MCP Hub-Spoke Architecture

Giving AI Agents Safe Access to OpenShift Clusters at Fleet Scale

Raghu Banda·Red Hat OpenShift AI
Red Hat
The Problem

AI agents can now manage clusters — but can they do it safely?

kubectl
Agents get raw kubectl with overprivileged tokens — no guardrails
No audit
No standard way to distinguish AI actions from human actions in API logs
No limits
A runaway agent can flood the API server — no rate limiting, no circuit breaker
N clusters
Every cluster needs separate credentials, separate scripts, separate access control

The central challenge is not whether AI can control a cluster — it's whether it can do it safely and with accountability. Today, agents use brittle scripts or direct kubectl with overprivileged tokens. There's no rate limiting, no audit trail that distinguishes agent from human, and no way to control access across a fleet. MCP — Model Context Protocol — is the open standard that addresses this.

Architecture

How the MCP Gateway stack works — seven components, one job each

ComponentPlain EnglishNamespace
Gateway (Envoy)The front door — receives all requests, enforces security via pluginsmcp-system
MCPRouterThe inspector — reads every request and decides where to send itopenshift-operators
MCPBrokerThe catalog — builds the list of available tools during session setupopenshift-operators
MCP Server v0.3The worker — actually runs the tool and talks to the K8s APIocp-mcp-server
AuthorinoThe ID checker — validates your token (SA or JWT) on every requestkuadrant-system
LimitadorThe rate limiter — prevents any one agent from overwhelming the systemkuadrant-system
KeycloakThe identity provider — issues JWTs for external agents. Talks to the Gateway, not MCP serverskeycloak
Confidential: Red Hat associate and NDA partner use only. No further distribution
E2E Flow

Step 0 — The agent gets a token before anything else

  • On-cluster agent — already has a ServiceAccount token. No external call needed
  • External agent — calls Keycloak, gets a JWT via client_credentials grant (expires in 30 min, auto-refreshes)
  • No token? — Gateway returns 401 with a discovery URL. Agent learns where to authenticate, gets a token, retries
  • Key point — Keycloak talks to the Gateway (Authorino), not to individual MCP servers. MCP servers never validate tokens
Confidential: Red Hat associate and NDA partner use only. No further distribution
E2E Flow

Step 1 — Agent connects: session setup and tool discovery

  • Agent → Route → Envoy — POST /mcp with token and JSON-RPC 'initialize'
  • Envoy → MCPRouter — inspects the request, recognizes it as init, passes it through
  • Envoy → Authorino + Limitador — token validated, rate limits checked
  • Envoy → MCPBroker — Broker creates session, discovers registered MCP servers, builds the unified tool catalog
  • Response — tool list + session ID returned. Agent now knows what tools are available
Confidential: Red Hat associate and NDA partner use only. No further distribution
E2E Flow

Step 2 — Agent calls a tool: routed directly to the MCP server

  • Agent → Route → Envoy — POST /mcp with token + session ID + tool call (e.g. 'list namespaces on sandbox602')
  • Envoy → MCPRouter — inspects request, sets routing header to target the correct MCP server, strips tool prefix
  • Envoy → Authorino + Limitador — same token + rate limit check as init
  • Envoy → MCP Server directly — Broker is NOT involved. Envoy routes straight to the MCP server using the headers MCPRouter set
  • MCP Server → K8s API — hub (local SA) or spoke (kubeconfig context). Returns real data back through the pipeline
Confidential: Red Hat associate and NDA partner use only. No further distribution
In Action

What does this look like in practice?

  • User: 'What pods are crashing in the autorag namespace?'
  • Agent calls: openshift_pods_list {namespace: autorag} → Gateway → Auth → MCP Server → K8s API
  • Agent answers: 'Two pods in CrashLoopBackOff: etcd-deployment (OOMKilled, 3 restarts) and milvus-standalone (exit code 1, 12 restarts)'
  • User: 'Are there any alerts firing?' → Agent calls openshift_get_alerts → '3 alerts: KubePodCrashLooping (2), NodeMemoryPressure (1)'
  • User: 'List namespaces on spoke cluster sandbox602' → Agent calls openshift_namespaces_list {context: sandbox602} → real spoke data returned through the full pipeline

Security

What happens when something goes wrong?

  • No token → Gateway returns 401 'Authentication required'. Request never reaches the MCP server
  • Invalid or expired token → Authorino rejects it. 401 returned. Logged in audit trail
  • Too many requests → Limitador returns 429. Per-user: 30/10s burst, 500/1h sustained. Global: 100/10s
  • Agent tries to read Secrets → MCP Server has denied_resources configured. Request blocked before it hits K8s API
  • Agent tries to delete something → MCP Server is read-only by default. Write operations must be explicitly enabled by the admin
Confidential: Red Hat associate and NDA partner use only. No further distribution
Multi-Cluster

Multi-cluster — one hub, many spokes, same tools everywhere

  • The MCP server sits on the RHACM hub — agents query any managed cluster from a single endpoint
  • Hub (default) — MCP Server uses a local ServiceAccount with read-only access. No kubeconfig needed
  • Spokes — tool calls with a context argument route to the right cluster via mounted kubeconfig. Keycloak token exchange is the roadmap for fully dynamic access
  • Adding a spoke — import into RHACM, create read-only SA on spoke, extract token, update hub config. Zero Gateway or auth changes
  • Everything upstream is spoke-agnostic — Gateway, Router, Broker, Authorino don't know or care if the target is hub or spoke
Confidential: Red Hat associate and NDA partner use only. No further distribution
